narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in traditional practices and identity. Although specific information on hairstyles during this era is scarce, it is known that protective hairstyles were a crucial part of Afro-textured hair care to minimize breakage and damage from environmental elements. Cornrows, a traditional hairstyle originating from Africa, were likely popular among Black women as they are considered a timeless and versatile style. The afro, which would later become a defining feature of the African-American culture in the 1960s, may not have gained widespread popularity yet, but its creation by combing out natural growth or styling with chemical curling products laid the groundwork for future generations to celebrate their kinky hair. Unfortunately, documentation from this era is limited, and more research is needed to provide a comprehensive understanding of hairstyles and hair culture during the 1940s.
